items.content:
The best way to get good at AI is ridiculously simple

Just hold Shift & YAP. Let me show you:

Step 1. Go to wispr .ai. Download it for free.
Step 2. Open Settings → General → Shortcuts.
Step 3. Pick your activation key. I use Shift.
Step 4. Open Claude. Hold Shift. Start yapping.

Not for 30 seconds. Not a clean, polished prompt.

Yap for 3 minutes straight. Minimum.

Talk about what you know.
The pain points you've seen at work.
The mistakes your clients keep making.
The stories only you can tell.

Don't organize & outline. Don't think about hooks.
Just rant like you're venting to a friend.

Step 5. End your rant with this exact line:

"These were all my messy thoughts.
I want to turn this into a LinkedIn post.
Don't find context outside of what I said.
Help me structure it. Put it in the right order.
Start by asking me questions."

Step 6. Answer Claude's questions with 'Shift' key.
Step 7. Claude writes the post. You edit hard.

That's the whole workflow.

Here's why this works and prompting doesn't:

When you type a prompt, you outsource thinking AND execution to AI.
When you yap, you only outsource the execution.

The thinking is yours. The stories are yours.
AI doesn't have your 10 years of experience. You do.

That's why your posts sound robotic and mine don't.

Three things about Wispr Flow that I personally love:

→ It strips your "ums" and "ahs" automatically.
→ It learns your words. Correct it once. It remembers forever.
→ You can whisper. So even at work, it works.

Your prompt is 500 words you agonized over.
Mine is 3 minutes of yapping.

The magic was never the prompt. It was the rant.

Writing emails from scratch in 2026 is embarrassing

Here's what I do instead (only takes 2 minutes):

Step 1. Install Granola. ai. It's free. 
→ It silently transcribes every Zoom/Teams/Meet call you join. No bot creeping in your meeting. 
→ People talk normally & you get the real conversation. Always open Granola when in calls.
(To gather the context of all your meetings.)

→ Settings > Connector > Connect Gmail + Granola
→ Claude can now read your inbox AND meeting transcripts at the same time. 
→ Most people connect just Gmail. It's not enough.

→ Note the sender + the meeting it ties to. 
→ This step is what makes the prompt 10x sharper.

Step 5. Ask Claude to "save as draft."
→ It lands in your Gmail. 0 copy and paste. You just open Gmail, review it, and hit send.

✦ Don't know how to build one? Take mine:
✦ Go to how-to-ai.guide. Subscribe for free.
✦ Don't pay anything. Open my welcome email.
✦ Hit the automatic reply button inside.
✦ Open the Notion link. Go to "Claude skills".
✦ Download the library. Upload it in Customize.

6. Turn every setting off. Empty your global instructions. Leave Connectors on. That's it.

8. Here's where most people quit reading. The longer your chat, the dumber it gets. Anthropic's own engineers said it out loud.

9. So stop typing "no, I meant…". Click "Restart the conversation from here" on an earlier message. 

10. A token is roughly one word. Every word you send & receive is money. Message 30 costs you 31 times message 1.

11. Point Fable 5 at your single hardest problem. Two turns. Then switch models. Turns are the most expensive habit you have.

12. Opus 5 High for everything else. High, not Max.

21. Ask for five very different versions. Then pick one. That part is taste, and taste is the part it can't do for you.

22. Make it audit its own answer before you trust a single line.

23. Feed it too much context and it goes in circles. Same answers every time, zero creativity. Keep the context in the project and the chat clean.

24. The first draft is yours to fix, not to ship. Always.

25. The only rule that matters: outsource the thinking, never the understanding.

Don't post (obvious) AI-written content.

Here are 12 tells to delete & the 11 skills that fix it:

(all 11 skills are free here → how-to-ai.guide)

Delete these from your writing today-

1. "Delve." You've never said it out loud. Once.
2. "Crucial/pivotal." Nothing is that pivotal.
3. "Tapestry." No human speaks like this.
4. "Here's the thing." There is no thing.
5. "Hope this helps." It doesn't. It outs you.
6. "After careful consideration." without considering
7. "to provide a quick update." Just give the update.
8. "Most people…" The lazy oversimplification.
9. "Robust / seamless / realm." The corporate AI.
10. Adverb abuse. "X quietly runs Y." Nothing runs.
11. "It's not X, it's Y." The famous AI sentence alive.
12. 'This isn't a budget. It's a statement of intent' No

Now my personally used 11 Claude skills that fix it:

1. /writer
Writes the first draft in your structure, not Claude's.
Good draft in = nothing to clean up later.

2. /editor
Cuts the fluff and the filler.
Every sentence earns its place or dies.

3. /fact-checker
Kills invented stats and fake-sounding quotes.
One hallucinated number and nobody trusts you again.

4. /anti-AI style
The base rewrite. Breaks the robotic rhythm 
where every sentence is the same 18 words.

5. /ban-the-AI-words
Auto-blocks "delve," "crucial," "tapestry"
& the entire red list above.

6. /ban-the-AI-patterns
Kills "It's not X, it's Y" and the fake-deep endings.
The patterns out you faster than the words do.

7. /sound like your posts
Feed it 5 of your old posts. It writes like YOU, not like Claude. This one replaces every "humanizer" tool you've paid for.

8. /humanizer
Strips whatever AI smell is left.
Contractions in, em dashes out.

9. /red-pen
Flags your weak lines before your readers do.

10. /self-critique
Claude critiquing Claude beats Claude on the first try. It loops until the text reads clean.

11. /auto-block-banned-words
The safety net. Nothing on the red list ever ships again.

That's the whole setup. 
12 tells deleted. 11 skills. 0 AI smell.

Extract the best creator in your niche instead.

So find the person whose LinkedIn you wish was yours (30+ posts, real engagement). You're not copying them. You're showing Claude what "great" looks like in your world - before you feed it yours.

—

STEP 3: Make Claude do math, not vibes.

Upload the Excel and tell it: "Compute the exact stats in code. Don't guess."

This is where 99% of people get fake answers, because the spreadsheet lies:

→ The real format is in which media columns are.
→ The date is inside each post's activity ID. Claude can decode it - you never would.
→ For image & carousel, ask Claude to OPEN media & look. Never let it judge a post from the caption.

a REPORT (what wins & why) and an SOP (the exact recipe for your next post).

New chat on Claude → type / → invoke your skill.

One invocation = one post. Every week.

items.content:
How to master Claude Fable 5 in only 15 steps:

(Send it to your team. They're burning credits)

1. Pick one super hard, expensive problem.
"Rewrite this email" is shooting a bird with a bazooka. Bring Fable a hard decision, a research report, a mess only a genius untangles.

2. Open a new Claude chat.
Fable re-reads the entire thread with every message - and you pay for every re-read. 
New task, new chat. No exceptions.

3. Select Fable 5 → Effort High.
Save "Max" effort for the truly brutal jobs. 
Thinking time costs credits too.

4. Paste your "about-me" doc.
AI is average by default - trained on everyone, so it answers like everyone. Keep one Google Doc: who you are, what you do, how you write. Paste it first.

5. Give it your goal, not a task.
The template: "I need [task] for [goal]. I expect [goal] achieved once we hit [specific targets]."

6. Add to the first prompt: "Ask me questions first."
Exact Prompt: "Start by asking me questions about the task, goal & targets to fully understand the context."

7. Add this to a prompt: "Answer first, explain after."
Now the first sentence of every follow up prompt is the bottom line. No more scrolling through methodology to find your answer.

8. Add: "Don't say done. Prove it."
Exact prompt: "Only report work you can point to evidence for. If something is not verified, say so."
This removes the fake "all done!" reports. Same standard you'd hold a new hire to.

9. Add: "Pick one option. Commit."
Exact prompt: "When you have enough information to act, act. Give me a recommendation, not a survey of options." You want a verdict, not a menu.

10. Send it. Answer its questions.
It asks 3-4 sharp ones. This 2-minute interview decides the quality of everything after.

11. Let it work. Don't interrupt.
Every "oh wait, also-" makes it re-read the whole thread. I paid $14 for one chat learning this.

12. Stop after 2 messages.
Fable's job is the genius part: the plan, the strategy, the hard call. That's it.

13. Switch to Opus 4.8 (High). Same chat.
Model menu → switch. Opus is included in your plan & it reads everything Fable just planned.
(Cowork can't switch mid-chat. Annoying, I know)

14. Finish everything there.
Drafts, edits, the 20-message back-and-forth: all on Opus. That's the free part.

15. Save it all in a Project.
Your files and instructions live there permanently. Tomorrow's session starts warm, not from zero.

Fable 5 thinks for 2 prompts. Opus 4.8 does the rest

----

One last thing.

I built a Skill that writes these prompts FOR you.
It's called /fable-prompter. You hand it a lazy idea. 
It gives you an optimised prompt.

Here's how to get it (takes 3 minutes):

1. Subscribe to my free newsletter: how-to-ai.guide.
2. You will receive an email. 
3. Click the Notion Library link mentioned inside. 
4. The /fable-prompter file is inside.
5. Go to Claude settings → Skills ("Capabilities").
6. Click + and upload the file. Toggle it on.
7. Open a chat. Type /fable-prompter + your idea.

items.content:
The optimization tool says to cut safety stock.  The risk is low.  The math is sound.

Nobody cuts it.

Not because they disagree with the model.  Because two years ago they took the blame for a stockout, and excess inventory sits in a nebulous bucket on the balance sheet.

That asymmetry is the whole story.  A stockout has a date, a customer, and a name attached to it.  Excess has none of those.  It's a line on a balance sheet that never gets traced back to a person or a decision.  So planners protect against the outcome that gets them called into a room, and the tool becomes something to override, not use.

You see the same instinct on the floor.  A site would rather see material piled in front of a critical machine than trust a number telling them they don't need it.  The pile is visible.  The carrying cost isn't.

What they're buying is protection against variation that would be a historic outlier...insurance against an event that hasn't happened in years, priced at whatever working capital costs.

Optimization doesn't fail on math.  It fails because the pain of the past outweighs the will to optimize.

items.content:
When a forecast misses and the product has a long lead time, organizations reach for the magic word…”EXPEDITE”.

Here’s what that actually costs.

I had a sterilization queue I could push a SKU through faster when we needed it. It worked. The product showed up. What wasn’t immediately apparent is that every other product sitting in that queue got delayed to make room.

Expediting feels like a safety valve. In reality, it’s an exchange. The disruption doesn’t disappear, it moves to someone else’s product line, and almost nobody traces it back to the original forecasting miss that caused it.

This is why “we can always expedite” is one of the most expensive sentences in supply chain. It’s true in isolation and false in aggregate. The capacity to expedite is finite, shared, and invisible until you’re the one waiting behind someone else’s emergency.

If your SIOP process treats expediting as a free recovery option instead of a cost with a real budget, you’re not planning…you’re borrowing against the future.

#SIOP #SupplyChain #ForecastAccuracy

items.content:
We launched a strategic project to improve delivery performance.

First finding: nobody could say what our delivery performance actually was.

Every site self-reports.  No metric standard.  One site measures against request date.  Another measures against promise date...and gives itself a 7-day grace period after the promise.  Same company, same metric name, multiple different definitions.  Every number in every review deck was true by its own rules and comparable to nothing.

So we collected the data manually across a subset of plants.  Two things became obvious fast: the volume can't be managed by someone on top of their day job, and Excel can't hold it.

Here's the part that should sound familiar.  The data exists.  Every order, every promise date, every ship date is sitting in our systems right now.  It's not a data problem, it's an access problem.  And the IT investment to fix access has been sitting in approval for months, while the strategic project that depends on it moves forward anyway.

That's the pattern: companies fund the initiative because initiatives are visible.  The data plumbing underneath is invisible...right up until you discover your sites have been grading their own homework with different answer keys.

You can't improve what you measure six different ways.

items.content:
A clinician orders a device at 11am expecting it tomorrow.

What they don't see: the unit took 18 days to manufacture, ship, and clear sterilization before it could even be in stock to ship.

Sales defaulted to the obvious assumption: high-runners drive the business, focus the forecast there.

They were wrong.  The actual demand drivers were the traditionally lower-volume SKUs...and sales had the signal.  Customer conversations showed it.  They just never said it out loud in the SIOP meeting, because they didn't see that meeting as where demand intelligence was supposed to land.

This is what people miss about SIOP: it's not a forecasting exercise, it's a demand intelligence pipeline.  With an 18-day lead time, there's no recovering from a miss at the shipping dock...the recovery window closed weeks earlier.

Same-day delivery promises don't fail at the dock.  They fail in a meeting Sales didn't think mattered.

-Director of SIOP & Global Inventory Management. Writing about what actually breaks SIOP, from inside it.

items.content:
The fastest way to kill a SIOP process isn't in a bad forecast.

It's one sentence: "I'm not sure that data is right."

Here's how it plays out.  the SIOP numbers get compiled manually.  Usually one person, one spreadsheet, every month.  Then a function walks into the meeting with their own dashboard that slices the data differently.  Something appears they don't like.  So they challenge the data itself.

No refuting data.  No alternative number.  Just doubt.

And it works...because doubt is asymmetric.  The challenge takes five seconds.  Proving the data was right takes two weeks, and by then the meeting has moved on and the decision didn't get made.  A manager told me years ago: everyone reads the headline, no one reads the retraction on page 6.

The damage isn't that one number got questioned.  It's that the process itself is now suspect.  Next month, every uncomfortable finding gets the same treatment...because the precedent is set that data you don't like can be dismissed instead of disproven.

The fix isn't a better spreadsheet.  It's a rule: challenges to the data require data.  If you can't bring a number, the number on the screen stands.

#SIOP #SupplyChain #SalesAndOperations #DataDriven

items.content:
Sales has two forecasts.

The one they commit to their leadership.  And the one they hand to SIOP.

The number they give sales leadership is conservative because that number has consequences.  Miss it and there's no bonus, no high fives, no place to hide.

The number they give SIOP is inflated because that number has none.  If supply chain builds to it and demand doesn't show, the disappointment lands on the SIOP team, the inventory lands on ops metrics, and sales absorbs exactly nothing.

I've sat in leadership meetings and heard it said out loud: "We're driving to X, but think we'll hit Y."

Here's what that tells you: sales can forecast just fine.  They forecast precisely as accurately as each audience can hold them accountable.  The inflated SIOP number isn't a skill problem, it's a rational response to a process with no teeth.  Infinite inventory means never missing a potential sale, and there's no downside charged to the people asking for it.

So before you buy forecasting software or run another accuracy workshop, ask one question: what happens to sales when the SIOP number misses?

If the answer is "nothing", you don't have a forecast.

You have a wish list.
